text:
The `bitcoind`, `electrum` and `stratum_v1` services are `json-rpc`, versions 1 and 2 and over `tcp`, `http`, and `websockets`. These are materially different from a REST interface, and share a common parse mechanism. I'm getting close to completion of the `json-rpc` parser that can drop into the above transport services allowing us to seamlessly support these as well. `websockets` and `http` processing are facilitated by `boost::beast` and with this parser, implementation of the API's is straightforward. `stratum_v1` is a proprietary interface, so it just ends up with a custom parser, similar to the `json-rpc` implementation. Finally `tls` can be transparently layered over all of these using the same implementation.

So for now I've activated the endpoints, and a couple are useful. I'll be adding to these rapidly. Presently this is all implemented in `libbitcoin-network` apart from settings parsing, which is in `libbitcoin-node`, but as soon as I start implementing store queries it all all move up to node. Eventually we'll probably move the endpoint specific behavior into a new `libbitcoin-server`, leaving the primitives (e.g. the parsers and base types) in network.

Completed the `json::rpc::request` parser and `json::rpc::response` serializer, as well as a `json::rpc::request` serializer to facilitate test. Good test coverage, but I'll add a bunch more tomorrow. This also includes the type system and a reader/writer `json::body<parser>` for `boost::asio::async_read` and `::async_write`, which utilizes the `request` parser and `response` serializer.

The serializers are straightforward writes to a stream buffer. Currently this uses `std::ostringstream`, but the performance of this could be bumped up using `system::ostream`, as we do with p2p network and store.

The parser is streaming, so can accommodate `boost::asio` piecemeal asynchronous buffer updates for a given request. Additionally the parser is non-allocating apart from the final copy/move of buffer values to the `request` object fields. Instead of pushing characters into a buffer, it moves views over the network buffer.

I've dusted off the `boost::json` declarative serialize/deserialize that was formerly applied to all of the chain objects (and actually reimplemented both of the above serializers with it but decided in favor of the custom implementation). These conversions are almost entirely declarative and very performant.

This will be used to convert the `request.params` object or array types from string blobs passed via in the json-rpc request/response DOM between the `channel`/`proxy` and the `protocol` implementations. As I outlined in the meeting, this deferred serialization simplifies the rpc layer, keeping native objects from being unnecessarily parsed in/out of a document object model.

Just as with `http::request` and `http::response` objects, we'll pass these `json::request` and `json::response` objects via a message distributor template instance for the various `json-rpc` based channels. Protocols just subscribe and handle the request, sending the response - just as with the p2p protocols.

elements.text: So there is a master network strand, which drives the connection process, and protects shared resources, like the address pool and certain config, and there is a strand for each channel. These all operate on the single network thread pool. There is only one other thread pool, which is to isolate CPU intensive prevout query and script validation. The database is synchronous and lock-free, so all database calls are just simple function calls from strands on either of these pools. Channels directly read/write the store, with the major block commitments coming concurrently from the channels that downloads the blocks.

elements.text: The important observation is that despite having each channel on the same thread pool, logically they operate entirely independently, with the strand ensuring thread safety only internally to the channel. There are also
chaser

objects that manage cross-channel state computations, such as performance deviations and validation. These also operate on their own strands and on the network thread pool, but are generally very low cost (apart from the aforementioned script validation, which uses an independent pool). So given that these are already logically independent (concurrent) logical strands of execution within a single thread pool, it is trivial to factor them into independent thread pools - based on NIC selection.

This is basically running a load balanced internally. This can be applied externally as well, but the OS doesn't do this.

And in that case there is a potential complexity, as one endpoint may be listening for various types of requests. Someone might post a JSON object or a document request for example. Also a protocol sends an response object but based on the requester's accept types, or query string, the response will need distinct encoding. A transaction may arrive as json or as text (hex) or as binary (wire). One might be returned in any of these formats as well. Due to the above-mentioned lack of polymorphism, dispatching in these cases can create a combinatorial type explosion. We would need to listen for headers, parse them and dispatch to another listener to read/parse the body into a certain format and construct a different request type using the header object and unique body type (e.g. json, string, data, file, empty).

boost::beast::http
bodies):

This is just a passthrough wrapper for each body type that selects the body type (parser) on request construct, based on the parsed request header. On the response the body is the response content (typed by the responder, including header content-type) and on writer construct the body serializer is selected for emitting the object. So we can pass around this single type which at almost no runtime cost passes through to a single contained type with parser/serializer automatically selected based on declared content-type.

I completed the integration of the new variant request/response types into `network::http_channel` and `network::http_protocol`. This enables `node::protocol_explore` and `node::protocol_html` receipt of any `http::request` contained variant type at the same endpoint, and the ability to construct and send back any `http::response` contained variant type. This code barely changed, all it required was replacement of `http::string_request` and `http::string_response` with the corresponding variant types. Sending doesn't require the variant type, it can just be sent with any type using polymorphism, works either way. But I expect that the variant response will end up becoming a useful mechanism for similar late branching of serialization if that becomes beneficial.

elements.text: Turns out the inflation from wire protocol to json is 2.5x, just based on pulling down some blocks in each format and comparing the file sizes. And even though we don't know the json size before we write it, and we need the buffer to do that, we can use the wire serialization size, which we get for free from the store-deserialized c++ instance of any object. For header this is just a static fixed value. But it varies a lot for others. So a 2.5x buffer estimate will eliminate most iteration over the buffer. Or we can accept a smaller number of iterations to preserve memory. Also resizing down is a cost in terms of reallocations, so there's always a tradeoff.

elements.text: The response time for p2p block output is certainly less than the data format above, despite having the same serialization, as there is no http overhead. So I think we can lay to rest any concerns about not being able to rapidly serve blocks to peers. If we had the blocks already stuffed on the SSD in wire serialization, they could maybe be served a tiny bit faster. But then of course every other query would be horrendous.
